This inverse 1 2 power-law relationship suggests that PUE is inversely proportional to approach temperature. As shown in Figure 17, when the approach temperature increases from 2 °C to 11 °C, PUE exhibits a significant reduction, indicating improved energy efficiency at higher approach temperatures because of the reduced power consumptions of the fan and coolant pump. The experimental test points show a strong fit to the inverse power-law trend with an R² value of 0.934, suggesting that 93.4% of the variability in PUE is explained by changes in the approach temperature. Particularly, the relationship is nonlinear, with the PUE decreasing rapidly between approach temperatures of 2 °C and 5 °C, indicating significant gains in energy efficiency within this range. Beyond 5 °C, the slope of the curve becomes more gradual, demonstrating diminishing returns in efficiency as the approach temperature increases further, with the trend stabilizing between 8 °C and 11 °C. The approach temperature is limited by the vapor high temperature as well as the minimum fan and coolant pump speeds. This implies that although higher approach temperatures improve PUE, the benefits decrease at higher values, potentially indicating an optimal operating range for maximizing energy savings. 20 Figure 17. MODELING 5.1 MODEL DESCRIPTION AND MAIN ASSUMPTIONS The present study introduces a semiempirical lumped model developed to predict the PUE of the 2PIC system. This model integrates fundamental energy conservation principles with empirical data-driven correlations, allowing for accurate predictions of core system metric—PUE. The 2PIC system is divided into two control volumes (CV1 and CV2) to simplify the energy analysis, as shown in Figure 18. Control Volume 1 (CV1) encompasses the heater and condenser, where the energy input from the heat load is balanced by the heat extracted by the circulating coolant. In Control Volume 2 (CV2), which includes the radiator, the energy balance considers the heat transferred from the coolant to the air through the radiator. 21 Figure 18.
